Age: 8 years  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Scald burns to anterior chest, abdomen, both upper extremities, and face after accidental spill of boiling water, presenting 45 minutes post‑injury with severe pain and distress.  

Analysis: All three experts agreed that the burn involves approximately 20 % total body surface area, calculated using the pediatric Lund‑Browder chart. The chest and abdomen exhibit superficial partial‑thickness burns (erythema with blisters), the forearms show deep partial‑ to full‑thickness injury (waxy, insensate skin), and the face has superficial burns. No clinical signs of inhalation injury or airway compromise were identified, though serial airway assessment is advised. Vital signs (HR 152, BP 94/58) indicate early compensated hypovolemic shock, supporting immediate fluid resuscitation per the Parkland formula (2 240 mL LR over 24 h, half in the first 8 h). Consensus also supports transfer to a verified pediatric burn center, IV morphine titrated for pain, wound cleaning with sterile saline, debridement of ruptured blisters, application of silver sulfadiazine to partial‑thickness areas, and preservation of deep forearm burns for surgical evaluation. Escharotomy is not indicated at this time. Continuous monitoring of vitals, urine output ≥1 mL/kg/h, pain, mental status, temperature, and laboratory studies is essential. No disagreements were noted among the experts; all responses were consistent.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Pulse oximetry, non‑invasive blood pressure cuff, continuous cardiac monitor, urinary catheter for output measurement, bedside ultrasound or clinical assessment for compartment syndrome, laboratory panel including CBC, electrolytes, BUN/creatinine, glucose, coagulation profile, and serial arterial blood gases if respiratory status changes; chest radiograph if airway edema develops.  

Conclusion: The patient requires emergent care for a major pediatric scald burn with mixed‑depth injuries, early fluid resuscitation, analgesia, and rapid transfer to a specialized pediatric burn center for definitive management.  

Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics  

Recommendations: Initiate Parkland‑guided lactated‑Ringer resuscitation immediately, delivering 1 120 mL in the first 8 hours from the time of injury and adjusting rate to maintain urine output ≥1 mL/kg/h. Provide IV morphine titrated to effect with frequent reassessment, supplemented by non‑pharmacologic comfort measures. Clean all burn areas with sterile saline, debride only ruptured blisters, apply silver sulfadiazine to superficial partial‑thickness zones, keep deep forearm burns moist and uncovered for early surgical consultation, and cover facial burns with a non‑adherent dressing. Maintain a warm ambient temperature and cover all burns to prevent hypothermia. Verify tetanus immunization status and administer tetanus toxoid if indicated. Begin early enteral nutrition with high‑calorie, high‑protein formulas to meet hypermetabolic demands. Provide psychological support through child‑life services and address parental anxiety. Monitor electrolytes closely for hyperkalemia from tissue breakdown and for hypocalcemia if transfusion becomes necessary. Avoid intramuscular injections in burned tissue. Perform serial airway assessments despite the absence of initial inhalation injury signs, watching for delayed edema. Consider a child‑abuse evaluation only if the history is inconsistent with the injury pattern.  

Notes: Continuous communication with the receiving pediatric burn center is essential to coordinate transfer, share fluid‑resuscitation data, and arrange for multidisciplinary care upon arrival.

Complaint: Persistent, excessive worry across multiple life domains for 8 months with associated restlessness, muscle tension, sleep difficulty, irritability, and concentration problems; partial benefit from meditation and exercise.  

Analysis: All three experts unanimously identified the presentation as meeting DSM‑5 criteria for Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) with a GAD‑7 score of 16 indicating severe anxiety. Consensus was reached that the case is non‑emergent and best managed within psychiatry. Experts agreed that thyroid dysfunction and stimulant use have been excluded by normal laboratory results and minimal caffeine intake. There was agreement that no additional medical work‑up is required unless new red‑flag symptoms appear. Points of divergence included: Expert A emphasized that no further diagnostics beyond the existing thyroid tests are needed, while Expert B and Expert C recommended routine screening for depression (PHQ‑9), substance use, and a brief suicidal ideation assessment. Expert B highlighted the need for pharmacotherapy in addition to psychotherapy given the severity, whereas Expert C focused on the necessity of a formal psychiatric evaluation before initiating medication. All experts concurred on the importance of lifestyle measures and the appropriateness of outpatient referral.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Physical examination (already performed), thyroid function panel (already performed), PHQ‑9 depression questionnaire, substance‑use screening questionnaire (e.g., AUDIT‑C), brief suicidal ideation risk assessment, urine pregnancy test if pregnancy is possible, baseline metabolic panel (CBC, CMP) and liver function tests prior to initiating an SSRI/SNRI, and optional urine drug screen if clinically indicated.  

Conclusion: Severe Generalized Anxiety Disorder requiring non‑emergent, outpatient psychiatric care.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Psychiatry  

Recommendations: Initiate a combined treatment plan that includes referral to a qualified mental‑health professional for cognitive‑behavioral therapy and consideration of a first‑line SSRI or SNRI after confirming pregnancy status and reviewing any contraindications. Prior to medication start, obtain baseline CBC, CMP, and liver function tests; document any prior exposure or adverse reactions to anxiolytics or antidepressants. Implement lifestyle augmentation: limit caffeine further, maintain regular aerobic exercise, practice sleep hygiene, and add progressive muscle relaxation or mindfulness techniques. Conduct screening for comorbid depression (PHQ‑9) and substance use, obtain a brief suicidal ideation assessment, and gather detailed family psychiatric history, social support evaluation, work and parenting stressors, and screen for past trauma or abuse. Assess for over‑the‑counter sleep aids or herbal supplements and inquire about chronic pain symptoms such as tension‑type headache. Schedule follow‑up in 4–6 weeks to titrate medication, evaluate efficacy and side effects, and reassess functional impairment; earlier contact (1–2 weeks) if adverse effects emerge. If sleep disturbance persists, consider formal sleep study. Repeat thyroid or endocrine testing only if clinical picture changes.  

Notes: Maintain documentation of all assessments, patient preferences, and informed consent for pharmacotherapy.

Analysis: The panel unanimously identifies allergic (IgE‑mediated) rhinitis as the most likely diagnosis based on chronicity, classic symptom pattern, trigger by indoor dust, and characteristic physical findings. All experts agree that the condition is non‑emergent and that Otolaryngology (ENT) is the appropriate subclinical specialty for management. Consensus points include dust‑mite exposure as the probable allergen, the need for intranasal corticosteroid therapy, and implementation of environmental control measures. Divergence appears in three areas: (1) timing of specialist referral – Experts A and B favor early ENT (and possible allergy) referral, whereas Expert C recommends primary‑care management initially; (2) scope of pharmacologic therapy – Expert A emphasizes intranasal corticosteroids alone, Expert B adds a second‑generation oral antihistamine and saline irrigation, and Expert C limits recommendation to intranasal steroids; (3) role of allergy testing – Experts A and B advocate skin‑prick or specific‑IgE testing early to confirm triggers, while Expert C considers testing optional and deferred until refractory disease or immunotherapy consideration. All agree on follow‑up within 4–6 weeks, though only Expert B specifies use of a validated rhinitis control questionnaire (RCAT).

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Nasal endoscopy (if structural concerns arise), skin‑prick testing or serum specific IgE for indoor allergens (dust mites), complete blood count with differential (optional to assess eosinophilia), spirometry (if lower‑airway symptoms develop), pregnancy test (if applicable), and validated symptom control questionnaire (RCAT).

Conclusion: The presentation is most consistent with chronic allergic rhinitis, likely driven by dust‑mite exposure, without current complications such as sinusitis, nasal polyps, or asthma.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)

Recommendations: Initiate a daily intranasal corticosteroid spray using proper technique and monitor for local side‑effects such as dryness or epistaxis; add a second‑generation oral antihistamine to address sneezing and rhinorrhea and consider isotonic saline nasal irrigation to improve mucociliary clearance. Implement comprehensive dust‑mite control: encase pillows and mattresses in allergen‑proof covers, wash bedding weekly in hot water, reduce indoor humidity below 50 %, remove wall‑to‑wall carpet if feasible, use a HEPA‑filter vacuum, and employ HEPA air cleaners. Arrange allergy testing (skin‑prick or specific‑IgE) to confirm dust‑mite sensitization and to guide potential future allergen immunotherapy; testing may be deferred if the patient achieves control with medication and avoidance. Schedule a follow‑up visit in 4–6 weeks, using the Rhinitis Control Assessment Test (RCAT) to quantify symptom improvement and to assess adherence and spray technique. If symptoms remain uncontrolled after optimal therapy, or if nasal polyps, chronic sinusitis, or asthma signs emerge, refer promptly to Otolaryngology (ENT) and consider collaboration with Allergy/Immunology for immunotherapy. Counsel the patient on the risk of progression to asthma (allergic march) and on monitoring for lower‑airway symptoms; advise spirometry if respiratory complaints develop. Review medication safety, noting that intranasal steroids are generally safe in pregnancy but should be used at the lowest effective dose, and that antihistamines have varying pregnancy categories. Assess for comorbid atopic conditions such as allergic conjunctivitis or atopic dermatitis, and obtain a family history of atopy to reinforce the allergic etiology. Ensure occupational exposures (e.g., cleaning agents) are evaluated as potential contributors to non‑allergic rhinitis. Emphasize the importance of adherence, correct spray technique, and regular environmental measures to sustain long‑term control.

Notes: Clarify pregnancy status before prescribing; document adherence and technique at each visit; consider spirometry and repeat endoscopic evaluation if new lower‑airway or sinus symptoms appear.

Age: 16 years  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Fever, sore throat, difficulty swallowing, fatigue, cervical lymphadenopathy, exudative pharyngitis with soft‑palate petechiae, and a faint macular rash on trunk and arms for one week  

Analysis: All three experts converged on a diagnosis of infectious mononucleosis caused by Epstein‑Barr virus (EBV) based on the classic triad of prolonged fever, exudative pharyngitis with soft‑palate petechiae, generalized cervical lymphadenopathy, and a macular rash that appeared without a documented prior antibiotic exposure. The experts agreed that the presentation lacks red‑flag features such as airway compromise, hemodynamic instability, rapidly enlarging neck mass, or severe abdominal pain, supporting a non‑emergent classification. Consensus differed in two areas: Expert C initially described the case as emergent because of the patient’s bedridden status, but the final round aligned with the majority that the case is non‑emergent; and there was a note that the rash could represent a reaction to an undocumented antibiotic (e.g., amoxicillin), which was not part of the initial differential but is acknowledged as a possible factor. Additional considerations raised during the rounds include potential splenomegaly, mild transaminitis, risk of secondary bacterial throat infection, atypical lymphocytosis as a diagnostic clue, possible false‑negative heterophile test in the first week, and the need to consider hepatitis B/C and HIV testing when risk factors exist.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Vital‑sign monitor, stethoscope for airway and respiratory assessment, otoscope for oropharyngeal inspection, measuring tape or ruler for cervical node size, hand‑held abdominal percussion for splenomegaly, CBC with differential, heterophile antibody (Monospot) test, EBV VCA IgM/IgG serology if Monospot negative, rapid streptococcal antigen test or throat culture, liver function panel (ALT, AST, bilirubin), HIV screen if risk factors, hepatitis B and C serologies if indicated, and optional CMV IgM/IgG serology if EBV testing remains negative.  

Conclusion: The most likely diagnosis is infectious mononucleosis due to Epstein‑Barr virus.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Infectious Disease  

Recommendations: Perform a focused bedside assessment including vital signs, airway patency, respiratory effort, thorough oropharyngeal examination, measurement of cervical lymph node size, palpation for splenomegaly, hydration status, brief neurologic and skin examination, and assessment for any red‑flag signs. Obtain the laboratory panel outlined above; if the heterophile test is negative but clinical suspicion remains high, repeat it in 48‑72 hours or proceed to EBV serology and consider CMV serology. Evaluate liver enzymes and, when risk factors are present, screen for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV. Counsel the patient and family that the illness is viral, typically self‑limited over 1–3 weeks, and emphasize strict activity restriction, avoiding contact sports for three to four weeks to prevent splenic rupture. Advise adequate hydration, use of acetaminophen or ibuprofen for fever and pain, throat lozenges, and rest. Warn about red‑flag symptoms such as worsening throat pain, drooling, stridor, respiratory distress, severe abdominal pain, jaundice, uncontrolled fever, or new rash, and instruct to seek immediate medical attention if they occur. Arrange outpatient follow‑up in seven to ten days to review symptom progression, CBC, and liver enzymes, and to re‑examine for splenomegaly or other complications; advise earlier return if any red‑flag signs develop. Reserve imaging (ultrasound or CT of neck/abdomen) for suspected peritonsillar or retropharyngeal abscess, airway compromise, or painful splenomegaly suggesting rupture. Avoid prescribing ampicillin or amoxicillin; if a bacterial superinfection is suspected, select an appropriate alternative antibiotic. Systemic corticosteroids are not indicated unless imminent airway obstruction develops; use NSAIDs cautiously if thrombocytopenia or significant liver dysfunction is present. Refer to ENT if an abscess is suspected, to infectious disease for prolonged fever beyond two weeks or atypical laboratory findings, to hematology for severe cytopenias or hemolysis, and to hepatology for marked transaminitis or jaundice.  

Notes: Monitor for complications including airway obstruction, splenic rupture, hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, hepatitis, and neurologic sequelae throughout the illness course.

Age: 4 years  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Rapidly progressive sore throat, dysphagia, drooling, noisy breathing, and toxic‑appearing distress  

Analysis: The child exhibits classic features of acute epiglottitis – high fever, drooling, tripod positioning, muffled “hot‑potato” voice, audible inspiratory stridor, and a thumb sign on lateral neck X‑ray confirming epiglottic swelling. All three experts unanimously diagnosed acute epiglottitis and agreed that the airway is imminently threatened, classifying the situation as a life‑threatening emergency that requires immediate intervention by anesthesiology and Otolaryngology (ENT). Consensus also identified Haemophilus influenzae type b as the most likely pathogen given the incomplete Hib immunization. Divergence among experts concerned the optimal intubation strategy: Expert A advocated inhalational induction with maintenance of spontaneous ventilation and avoidance of direct laryngoscopy, whereas Expert B recommended rapid‑sequence intubation with direct laryngoscopy for speed. Expert B additionally suggested empiric vancomycin for possible MRSA coverage, an option not raised by the other two experts. All agreed on the need for definitive airway control in a controlled environment, postoperative PICU admission, and empiric third‑generation cephalosporin therapy after airway security.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Portable pulse‑oximeter, continuous cardiac monitor, humidified high‑flow oxygen delivery system, pediatric difficult‑airway cart (including video laryngoscope, fiberoptic bronchoscope, appropriately sized endotracheal tubes, bougies, and cricothyrotomy set), operating‑room or intensive‑care‑unit setting for controlled intubation, lateral soft‑tissue neck X‑ray (already obtained), blood cultures, complete blood count, C‑reactive protein and other inflammatory markers (to be drawn after airway is secured).  

Conclusion: Acute epiglottitis with impending airway obstruction requiring emergent airway management and empiric antimicrobial therapy.  

Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)  

Recommendations: Maintain the child in the tripod position in a quiet, low‑stimulus environment and provide supplemental humidified oxygen without delaying airway intervention. Avoid any oral, nasopharyngeal, or tongue‑depressor examination until the airway is secured to prevent reflex laryngospasm. Proceed to definitive airway control in the operating room or PICU with both anesthesiology and ENT present; the team should be prepared to use either inhalational induction with spontaneous ventilation (as per Expert A) or rapid‑sequence intubation with direct laryngoscopy (as per Expert B) based on provider expertise and equipment availability, ensuring that a pediatric video‑laryngoscope or fiberoptic scope is ready. Have a surgical airway kit immediately available for emergent cricothyrotomy or tracheostomy if intubation fails. After successful intubation, obtain blood cultures, CBC, and inflammatory markers, then initiate intravenous ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime); add vancomycin if there is a high local prevalence of MRSA or other risk factors. Admit the patient to the pediatric intensive care unit for close monitoring of airway edema, hemodynamics, and potential complications such as sepsis or need for re‑intubation. Provide fluid resuscitation and electrolyte management only after airway stabilization. Counsel the family on the critical importance of completing the Hib vaccine series after recovery. Use corticosteroids only if institutional protocol supports their benefit, acknowledging that routine use remains controversial. Document all interventions, monitor for persistent airway edema, and reassess the need for continued ventilation or extubation readiness.  

Notes: Ensure all team members are briefed on the airway plan, equipment check, and backup surgical airway strategy prior to entering the operating suite.

Complaint: Persistent low mood, anhedonia, insomnia with early awakening, decreased appetite with 14‑lb weight loss, psychomotor retardation, feelings of worthlessness, poor concentration, social withdrawal for 2 months after a relationship breakup.

Analysis: All three experts agree that the patient meets DSM‑5 criteria for a major depressive episode and that the most appropriate primary diagnosis is Major Depressive Disorder, single episode, severe, without psychotic features. Consensus also confirms the absence of suicidal ideation, hallucinations, or delusions, and the lack of any immediate safety threat, supporting a non‑emergent care pathway. The experts uniformly recommend outpatient psychiatric management with prompt initiation of treatment. Points of divergence include: (1) the emphasis on a structured risk assessment – Expert B explicitly recommends it, whereas Experts A and C do not mention it; (2) the degree of urgency for follow‑up – Expert B suggests a 2‑4 week review, while Expert A provides a general favorable prognosis without a specific interval; (3) the necessity of laboratory evaluation – Experts A and B list a comprehensive metabolic panel, CBC, thyroid studies, and vitamin levels as standard, while Expert C notes the weight loss as a possible medical concern but is less definitive. These differences are reconciled by adopting a comprehensive medical work‑up and a brief risk assessment, followed by early outpatient follow‑up within 1‑2 weeks, with a more formal evaluation at 2‑4 weeks.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, thyroid‑stimulating hormone, vitamin B12 and folate levels, and a basic toxicology screen if clinically indicated.

Conclusion: The presentation is consistent with a first‑episode, severe major depressive disorder without psychotic features or suicidal intent, requiring timely outpatient psychiatric intervention and exclusion of medical contributors to depressive symptoms.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Psychiatry

Recommendations: Order the indicated laboratory studies to rule out endocrine, hematologic, or nutritional abnormalities that could mimic or worsen depression. Conduct a brief structured risk assessment focusing on suicidal thoughts, plans, means, and protective factors, documenting the negative findings. Initiate first‑line pharmacotherapy with an SSRI such as sertraline or escitalopram, starting at a low dose and titrating as tolerated. Refer the patient for evidence‑based psychotherapy, preferably cognitive‑behavioral therapy or interpersonal therapy, to address depressive cognitions and the recent relational loss. Schedule a rapid outpatient psychiatric follow‑up within 1‑2 weeks to assess medication tolerance, early response, and any emergence of suicidal ideation, with a more comprehensive evaluation at 2‑4 weeks. Coordinate with the primary care physician to obtain and review laboratory results and to monitor for any medical conditions that may require specialty referral. Provide psychoeducation on sleep hygiene, activity scheduling, and the importance of medication adherence.

Notes: Close monitoring is warranted given the severity of symptoms, marked weight loss, and psychomotor retardation, even though no acute safety concerns are present. The patient should be instructed to seek immediate care if suicidal thoughts, worsening mood, or any new psychotic symptoms develop.

Age: 72
Sex: Male
Complaint: Three days of vague periumbilical discomfort now localized to the right lower quadrant, decreased appetite, mild nausea, and one episode of loose stool.
Analysis: The clinical picture of pain migration, mild nausea, and anorexia together with CT findings of a 14 mm dilated appendix, peri‑appendiceal fat stranding and a small contained fluid collection is diagnostic of acute appendicitis with early (contained) perforation. All three experts agreed on this diagnosis, the need for emergent care, and that General Surgery is the appropriate specialty. Experts A and B uniformly recommend immediate operative management (laparoscopic appendectomy with possible drainage). Expert C highlighted that, in selected patients with a small contained collection, a brief trial of broad‑spectrum antibiotics with close monitoring could be considered, though surgical consultation remains essential. The panel also noted that elderly patients, especially those with diabetes, may have muted systemic signs (absence of fever, modest leukocytosis) and that comorbidities increase peri‑operative risk.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Contrast‑enhanced CT abdomen (already obtained), complete blood count with differential, basic metabolic panel, coagulation profile, serum electrolytes, renal function tests, ECG, cardiac enzymes, blood cultures if sepsis suspected, medication review (antiplatelet/anticoagulant use), allergy history to antibiotics and contrast, assessment of functional status for postoperative mobilization.
Conclusion: Acute appendicitis with early (contained) perforation in a 72‑year‑old man with type 2 diabetes and coronary artery disease.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: General Surgery
Recommendations: Initiate NPO status and begin intravenous crystalloid resuscitation; start broad‑spectrum antibiotics covering gram‑negative and anaerobic organisms (e.g., piperacillin‑tazobactam or ceftriaxone plus metronidazole) after obtaining blood cultures; obtain and review allergy history before antibiotic administration; obtain cardiac risk assessment (ECG, cardiac enzymes) and continue beta‑blocker therapy as indicated; optimize glucose control with insulin sliding scale or infusion; evaluate antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy and hold or reverse as clinically appropriate; assess renal function for dosing of antibiotics and contrast‑related considerations; admit to the surgical service for urgent evaluation. Proceed with urgent laparoscopic appendectomy with intra‑abdominal drainage of the contained fluid collection if feasible; if immediate surgery is contraindicated (e.g., uncorrectable anticoagulation, hemodynamic instability), consider initial non‑operative management with intravenous antibiotics, strict monitoring of vital signs, abdominal examinations, serial labs, and early conversion to surgery if clinical deterioration occurs. Provide venous thromboembolism prophylaxis tailored to recent knee replacement; ensure pain control that does not mask evolving abdominal signs; monitor for early sepsis despite normal temperature and modest leukocytosis; arrange postoperative early ambulation, continued antibiotic therapy, cardiac monitoring, and assessment for underlying malignancy on pathology; discharge planning should include wound care instructions, glucose management, activity restrictions, and clear criteria for return to care (fever, increasing pain, wound erythema). Schedule outpatient surgical follow‑up within 7‑10 days.
Notes: Elderly diabetic patients may present with atypical or muted symptoms; low‑grade leukocytosis does not exclude severe infection. A small contained collection may be amenable to laparoscopic drainage but still warrants surgical evaluation. Underlying cecal pathology (e.g., carcinoma) should be considered and will be evaluated on final pathology. Antiplatelet/anticoagulant therapy may affect timing of surgery and requires peri‑operative management. Renal function must be checked before contrast use and for antibiotic dosing. Functional status after recent knee replacement influences postoperative mobilization and VTE prophylaxis. Pain management should avoid oversedation that could hide worsening abdominal signs. Early sepsis assessment is essential even with normal vital signs.

Age: 29  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Eye fatigue, dryness, and mild headache that worsen with prolonged computer use and improve on weekends.  

Analysis: The panel unanimously identified digital eye strain (computer vision syndrome) as the most likely diagnosis, based on the temporal relationship of symptoms to screen time, normal visual acuity, intact extraocular movements, and only mild conjunctival injection. All experts agreed that there are no red‑flag findings, making the condition non‑urgent. Consensus differed on the immediacy of specialist involvement and diagnostic testing. Experts A and C recommended deferring referral and formal testing until after a trial of self‑care, whereas Expert B advocated for an early baseline refraction, slit‑lamp examination, and dry‑eye assessment. Similarly, Experts A and C suggested reserving tear‑film tests for refractory cases, while Expert B proposed performing them at the initial visit. All agreed on the importance of addressing ergonomic, environmental, and ocular surface factors, and on a follow‑up interval of 4–6 weeks.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: At the initial visit no mandatory tests are required; if symptoms persist after 4–6 weeks, consider a manifest refraction, slit‑lamp biomicroscopy, tear‑film breakup time or Schirmer test, and a binocular vision assessment (e.g., near point of convergence).  

Conclusion: The presentation is consistent with digital eye strain without emergent features. Initial management should focus on self‑care measures, with escalation to ophthalmology or optometry if symptoms do not improve.  

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: Ophthalmology  

Recommendations: Implement the 20‑20‑20 rule (every 20 minutes look at an object 20 feet away for 20 seconds) and take regular micro‑breaks to reduce accommodative load. Optimize workstation ergonomics by positioning the monitor at arm’s length with the top at or slightly below eye level, ensuring proper chair posture, and minimizing glare with appropriate lighting and screen filters. Adjust screen settings for comfortable brightness, contrast, and consider a blue‑light filter if it reduces discomfort. Use a humidifier in dry environments and maintain adequate hydration throughout the day. Apply preservative‑free artificial tears 2–4 times daily; add a lubricating ointment at night if dryness persists. Review any systemic conditions (e.g., autoimmune disease, thyroid dysfunction) and medications (e.g., antihistamines, antidepressants, isotretinoin) that may exacerbate dry eye, and modify them if possible. Assess stress levels, sleep quality, and overall posture, addressing these factors as contributors to the associated headache. If symptoms remain unchanged after 4–6 weeks of these measures, obtain a comprehensive eye examination including refraction and binocular vision testing, and consider referral to ophthalmology or optometry for further evaluation and possible treatment such as corrective lenses or targeted vision therapy. In refractory dry‑eye cases, a short course of preservative‑free topical cyclosporine A may be considered. Schedule a follow‑up visit in 4–6 weeks, with earlier review if any red‑flag symptoms (sudden vision loss, eye pain, photophobia, flashes, floaters, diplopia, severe headache, or neurological deficits) develop.  

Notes: Emphasize patient education on the importance of consistent break habits and ergonomic adjustments. Encourage communication with occupational health or a vision therapist for a formal workstation assessment if workplace constraints limit self‑implementation.

Age: 56  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Shortness of breath and cough of several days, preceded by rhinorrhea, with a chronic productive morning cough that has worsened over the past two days.  

Analysis: The panel converged on a diagnosis of chronic bronchitis, a phenotype of COPD, now presenting with an acute exacerbation likely triggered by a recent viral upper‑respiratory infection. The patient’s 40‑pack‑year smoking history, long‑standing productive cough, and seasonal worsening support this interpretation. All experts agreed that there are no immediate red‑flag symptoms such as hemoptysis, fever, chills, severe dyspnea at rest, or syncope, leading to the consensus that care is non‑emergent and best directed to pulmonology. Divergence arose from Expert C, who cautioned that the combination of heavy smoking and acute symptom change could mask pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, or early lung cancer despite the absence of overt red flags, and therefore suggested a more urgent evaluation. Additional considerations raised during the rounds include the need for pulse‑oximetry, assessment for alpha‑1 antitrypsin deficiency, mental health screening, cardiovascular comorbidity evaluation, occupational exposure history, COVID‑19 testing, up‑to‑date vaccinations, and potential need for home oxygen.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Chest radiograph (postero‑anterior and lateral), spirometry with bronchodilator response, pulse‑oximetry at rest, complete blood count, sputum culture if purulent sputum is noted, C‑reactive protein or erythrocyte sedimentation rate as inflammatory markers, low‑dose computed tomography for lung‑cancer screening, SARS‑CoV‑2 PCR or antigen test, alpha‑1 antitrypsin level if early‑onset COPD is suspected, electrocardiogram and, if indicated, echocardiogram for cardiac assessment, and a structured occupational exposure questionnaire.  

Conclusion: The most likely diagnosis is an acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis (COPD) in a current heavy smoker, with the need to exclude pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, and lung cancer through targeted testing.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology  

Recommendations: Arrange an outpatient visit within the next few days to obtain a chest X‑ray, spirometry, pulse‑oximetry, CBC, and inflammatory markers; consider sputum culture if sputum becomes purulent. Perform low‑dose CT screening for lung cancer in accordance with USPSTF criteria. Obtain a COVID‑19 test given recent upper‑respiratory symptoms. Initiate short‑acting bronchodilator therapy (e.g., albuterol) as needed and assess the need for a brief course of oral corticosteroids based on symptom severity. Prescribe antibiotics only if there is evidence of bacterial infection such as increased sputum purulence. Provide intensive smoking‑cessation counseling and refer to a cessation program. Update influenza, pneumococcal, and COVID‑19 vaccinations. Schedule a follow‑up appointment in 1–2 weeks to reassess symptoms, repeat pulse‑oximetry, and review test results. Refer to pulmonology for comprehensive COPD management, including long‑term inhaled therapy, pulmonary rehabilitation, and ongoing smoking‑cessation support. Screen for depression and anxiety, evaluate cardiovascular risk factors, and consider echocardiography if heart failure is suspected. Review occupational exposure history and test for alpha‑1 antitrypsin deficiency if clinical suspicion arises. If chronic hypoxemia is identified, evaluate the need for home oxygen therapy.  

Notes: Ensure patient education on recognizing red‑flag symptoms such as new onset fever, chest pain, hemoptysis, or worsening dyspnea that would warrant immediate medical attention.

Analysis: All three experts agreed that the presentation is classic for an acute viral upper respiratory infection (common cold) caused most often by rhinovirus. The patient is afebrile, well‑appearing, and lacks red‑flag findings such as high fever, dyspnea, facial pain, purulent discharge, cervical lymphadenopathy, or signs of systemic illness. The consensus diagnosis is acute viral rhinosinusitis (common cold) and the condition is self‑limited, typically resolving in 7–10 days. Minor areas of difference emerged: Expert A and C emphasized that isolation is not mandatory, whereas Expert B recommended home isolation for the contagious period (≈3‑4 days) and a return to work only after being fever‑free for 24 hours. Expert B also suggested optional primary‑care follow‑up if symptoms persist beyond 10 days, while Experts A and C mentioned follow‑up only for worsening or new symptoms. All experts concurred that no diagnostic testing or antibiotics are indicated in the current state.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None required for routine management. Consider rapid COVID‑19 or influenza testing only if fever develops, if there is high community prevalence, or if the patient has risk factors for complications.  

Conclusion: Acute viral upper respiratory infection (common cold) – self‑care appropriate.  

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine  

Recommendations: Provide symptomatic relief with adequate rest, hydration, saline nasal irrigation, and over‑the‑counter analgesics such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen as needed. Short‑term use of intranasal decongestant or antihistamine spray may be considered for nasal congestion. Emphasize strict hand hygiene, respiratory etiquette, and avoidance of close contact with vulnerable individuals. Because the patient works in a daycare, advise temporary home isolation for the first 3‑4 days of illness (the period of highest contagion) and a return to work only after being fever‑free for at least 24 hours and feeling sufficiently improved. Counsel the patient to monitor for red‑flag signs (fever >38.5 °C, new ear or facial pain, purulent nasal discharge, worsening sore throat, shortness of breath) and to seek medical evaluation if any develop or if symptoms persist beyond 10 days.  

Address additional considerations: Verify influenza and COVID‑19 vaccination status; if unvaccinated or if community transmission is high, discuss testing. Ask about a history of allergic rhinitis, asthma, smoking/vaping, pregnancy, and any medication allergies to tailor OTC medication choices. Document any immunocompromised conditions or chronic diseases that could alter the usual course. No antibiotics are indicated.  

Notes: Document the clinical assessment, reassurance provided, and the education on infection‑control measures. Arrange a follow‑up call or visit if the clinical course deviates from the expected 7–10 day resolution.

Age: 5 years  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Itchy red papules on forearms and lower legs after outdoor play  

Analysis: All three experts converged on the diagnosis of papular urticaria secondary to arthropod (insect) bites, citing the classic appearance of multiple small erythematous papules with central puncta on exposed skin, intense pruritus, recent outdoor exposure, and the absence of systemic signs. The panel uniformly agreed that the condition is non‑urgent and can be managed in primary pediatric care. Points of divergence were limited to the breadth of the differential diagnosis: Expert A and B explicitly listed urticaria multiforme, while Expert C placed it as a less common consideration; Expert A added contact dermatitis, scabies, viral exanthem, early impetigo, and urticaria; Expert B also included tick bite in endemic areas; Expert C highlighted the low probability of tick‑borne illness but recommended inquiry when appropriate. The extra considerations raised during the rounds (atopic background, recent product changes, family allergy history, immune status, environmental control, scabies, spider bites, and rare serious mimics) were not viewed as primary diagnoses but as contextual factors that could modify assessment or management.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: No routine laboratory or imaging studies are indicated for a typical presentation. Skin scraping may be performed if scabies is suspected; bacterial culture of any purulent discharge and a complete blood count are reserved for lesions with signs of secondary infection or systemic involvement.

Conclusion: Papular urticaria due to insect bites, a benign, self‑limited dermatosis.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics  

Recommendations: Provide symptomatic relief with oral antihistamines and low‑ to medium‑potency topical corticosteroids; apply cool compresses and keep fingernails trimmed to minimize scratching. Counsel the caregiver on preventive measures: regular use of insect repellent, wearing protective clothing, eliminating standing water, installing window screens, and inspecting the child for ticks after outdoor activities in endemic regions. Advise avoidance of known irritants and review any recent changes in soaps, detergents, or topical products that could suggest contact dermatitis. Inquire about a personal or family history of atopic dermatitis, severe allergies, or eosinophilic disorders, which may predispose to more pronounced reactions. Monitor for red‑flag signs (fever, rapidly spreading erythema, warmth, purulent drainage, lymphangitis, regional lymphadenopathy, joint pain, or anaphylaxis) and arrange prompt evaluation if they appear. Schedule follow‑up if lesions do not improve within 7–10 days, worsen, develop infection, or if new systemic symptoms emerge. Consider scabies if the rash becomes more numerous, involves intertriginous areas, or other household members are affected; perform skin scraping if indicated. Recognize that spider bites are unlikely given the absence of necrosis or severe pain, but remain aware of this possibility. Rare serious mimics such as early meningococcemia or vasculitis are improbable without systemic toxicity but should be reconsidered if the clinical picture changes.

Notes: Emphasize education on environmental control to reduce future insect exposure. Document any atopic or allergic history for future reference.

Age: 24 years  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Dysuria, urinary frequency, right flank pain, fever, rigors, nausea and vomiting  

Analysis: The patient’s presentation of dysuria, frequency, high fever (>102 °F), rigors, marked costovertebral angle tenderness, and urinalysis showing leukocyte esterase, nitrites, pyuria and bacteriuria is classic for acute pyelonephritis. Systemic signs (tachycardia, borderline hypotension, vomiting) indicate early sepsis, supporting the consensus that emergent care is required. All three experts agreed on the diagnosis, the need for emergency department evaluation, and inpatient admission for intravenous antibiotics and fluids. Consensus differed on the timing of imaging: Expert A advocated for early renal imaging in all cases, whereas Experts B and C recommended reserving imaging for lack of clinical improvement or suspicion of obstruction/abscess. The panel also diverged on the relevance of ectopic pregnancy: Experts A and B considered it highly unlikely given a negative point‑of‑care test, while Expert C, after reconsideration, endorsed obtaining a serum β‑hCG to definitively exclude pregnancy, including ectopic gestation.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Urine culture, blood cultures, complete blood count, basic metabolic panel, serum lactate, serum β‑hCG (if any doubt about pregnancy), sexually transmitted infection screening (chlamydia, gonorrhea), and renal ultrasound or CT abdomen/pelvis only if no improvement within 24–48 hours or if obstruction/abscess is suspected.  

Conclusion: Acute pyelonephritis with systemic involvement and early sepsis requiring emergent emergency‑department management and inpatient admission.  

Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Infectious Disease  

Recommendations: Initiate immediate intravenous fluid resuscitation to address possible dehydration from vomiting, and start empiric intravenous ceftriaxone 1–2 g daily, with alternatives such as cefotaxime, piperacillin‑tazobactam, or a fluoroquinolone if local antibiogram data support its use and there are no contraindications. Obtain urine and blood cultures before antibiotics to guide targeted therapy, especially given prior UTIs. Measure serum lactate to assess for early sepsis and monitor blood pressure and heart rate frequently to detect progression to septic shock. Perform a serum β‑hCG to definitively rule out pregnancy, including ectopic pregnancy, despite a negative rapid test. Screen for sexually transmitted infections as part of the broader work‑up. Defer renal imaging unless the patient fails to improve clinically within 24–48 hours, develops worsening flank pain, or shows signs of obstruction or abscess. Counsel the patient on signs of worsening infection (increasing fever, persistent vomiting, worsening pain, hypotension) that require immediate return to care. Provide education on adequate hydration, post‑coital voiding, proper genital hygiene, and avoidance of spermicidal products. Discuss the potential contribution of oral contraceptives to urinary stasis and consider alternative contraceptive methods if recurrent UTIs persist. Arrange follow‑up with primary care or urology within 48–72 hours of discharge, repeat urine culture after completion of antibiotics, and schedule outpatient renal imaging to evaluate for anatomic abnormalities that may predispose to future infections.  

Notes: Close coordination between emergency medicine, infectious disease, and urology is essential for optimal management and prevention of complications.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology

Notes: Ensure vaccination against herpes zoster (Shingrix) is discussed for future prevention once the acute episode resolves. Monitor for signs of secondary bacterial infection or ocular involvement if the ophthalmic branch is involved.

Age: 28 years  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Continuous generalized tonic‑clonic seizure activity lasting >12 minutes despite pre‑hospital and emergency department benzodiazepines  

Analysis: All three experts concur that the patient is in generalized convulsive status epilepticus that meets criteria for refractory status epilepticus because seizures persisted after an adequate dose of intramuscular midazolam (10 mg) and an intravenous lorazepam bolus (4 mg). The consensus identifies medication non‑adherence to levetiracetam as the primary precipitant, with fever as a possible co‑trigger (infection versus seizure‑induced hyperthermia). Life‑threatening complications are uniformly recognized: hypoxia, cyanosis, irregular respirations, hyperthermia, tachycardia, and hypertension, mandating immediate airway protection, hemodynamic support, and ICU admission. There is unanimous agreement on the need for rapid sequence intubation, avoidance of further benzodiazepines due to respiratory compromise, and prompt administration of a second‑line intravenous antiseizure medication (fosphenytoin, valproic acid, or levetiracetam loading). Diagnostic priorities (laboratory panel, neuroimaging, continuous EEG) are also shared.  

Points of divergence: Expert C highlighted additional gaps not emphasized by Experts A and B, specifically the need to monitor urine output and anticipate acute kidney injury from rhabdomyolysis, early nephrology involvement if creatine kinase rises markedly, consideration of therapeutic hypothermia protocols after intubation, formal seizure‑diary and adherence counseling after stabilization, and coordinated case‑management to address insurance‑related non‑adherence. Expert B suggested that a small repeat benzodiazepine dose (e.g., 1 mg lorazepam) could be given after airway security if seizures persist, whereas Experts A and C advised against further benzodiazepines. These nuanced differences are incorporated into the recommendations.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Rapid‑sequence intubation kit with video laryngoscope, mechanical ventilator, continuous cardiac monitor, non‑invasive blood pressure cuff, pulse oximeter, temperature probe, arterial line (if needed), point‑of‑care glucose meter, arterial blood gas analyzer, bedside laboratory analyzer for electrolytes, renal and hepatic panels, complete blood count, serum calcium, magnesium, phosphorus, creatine kinase, lactate, troponin, serum levetiracetam level, toxicology screen, pregnancy test, blood cultures, non‑contrast head CT scanner, continuous video EEG system, lumbar puncture set (for post‑imaging CSF analysis), urine output monitoring equipment, and therapeutic hypothermia device (optional).  

Conclusion: The patient is experiencing refractory generalized convulsive status epilepticus with imminent risk of respiratory failure, hemodynamic instability, and secondary complications; emergent airway protection, rapid seizure control with a second‑line antiseizure medication, and intensive care monitoring are required.  

Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Neurology  

Recommendations: Secure the airway immediately with rapid‑sequence intubation and initiate mechanical ventilation; provide 100 % oxygen and continuous cardiac monitoring; begin aggressive temperature control with antipyretics and external cooling; administer a second‑line intravenous antiseizure medication without delay (choose fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg, valproic acid 30 mg/kg, or levetiracetam 60 mg/kg, respecting maximum doses) and consider a single low‑dose lorazepam (1 mg) only after the airway is protected if seizures persist. Obtain emergent labs including ABG, comprehensive metabolic panel, CBC with differential, calcium, magnesium, phosphorus, CK, lactate, troponin, renal and hepatic function, serum levetiracetam level, toxicology screen, pregnancy test, and blood cultures. Perform non‑contrast head CT promptly; if imaging is negative and infection remains a concern, proceed with lumbar puncture after CT. Initiate continuous video EEG without delay to guide ongoing therapy. Monitor urine output hourly, track CK trends, and involve nephrology early if CK rises >5,000 U/L or renal function declines. Consider therapeutic hypothermia (target 33‑35 °C) if seizures remain refractory after second‑line therapy and airway is secured. Assess for aspiration pneumonia with chest imaging and start empiric antibiotics if clinically indicated. Evaluate for autoimmune encephalitis (e.g., anti‑NMDA receptor antibodies) given the patient’s age and refractory course; involve rheumatology or infectious disease as needed. Verify pregnancy status to tailor imaging and medication choices. After stabilization, arrange seizure‑diary education, adherence counseling, and social‑work case management to address insurance gaps and ensure medication access.  

Notes: Continuous reassessment of neurologic status, hemodynamics, and metabolic parameters is essential; adjust therapy based on EEG findings and laboratory results.

winner_protocol:
Age: 31  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Six‑month history of bilateral milky nipple discharge, amenorrhea for 6 months, progressive frontal/retro‑orbital headaches, weight gain, lethargy, decreased libido, and difficulty conceiving.  

Analysis: The patient presents with classic features of hyperprolactinemia—galactorrhea, amenorrhea, infertility, and elevated serum prolactin (500 µg/L). MRI demonstrates a sellar mass measuring 1.1 × 1.6 × 2.1 cm, confirming a pituitary adenoma. Consensus among the expert panel identifies this lesion as a prolactin‑secreting macroadenoma (prolactinoma) that requires prompt but non‑emergent care and specialist management by endocrinology. All experts agree on the diagnosis, the need for dopamine‑agonist therapy, and the importance of visual‑field testing and imaging follow‑up. Points of divergence include: Expert C described the lesion as a microadenoma despite one dimension >1 cm, whereas Experts A and B correctly classified it as a macroadenoma. Expert B emphasized macroprolactin (PEG precipitation) testing and a comprehensive pituitary hormone panel, while Expert A focused on the core work‑up. Expert B also recommended baseline cardiac echocardiography and bone mineral density assessment, concerns echoed in the additional considerations.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Serum prolactin level, macroprolactin (PEG precipitation) assay, full pituitary hormone panel (LH, FSH, estradiol, cortisol, ACTH, IGF‑1, TSH, free T4), serum chemistry (creatinine/eGFR, liver function tests), urine pregnancy test, contrast‑enhanced pituitary MRI, formal visual‑field perimetry, baseline transthoracic echocardiogram, dual‑energy X‑ray absorptiometry (DEXA) for bone mineral density, depression screening questionnaire, review of over‑the‑counter/herbal product use.  

Conclusion: Prolactin‑secreting pituitary macroadenoma (prolactinoma) causing hyperprolactinemia, galactorrhea, secondary hypogonadism, infertility, and headache. No acute visual compromise or apoplexy is present, allowing for scheduled, non‑emergent intervention.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology  

Recommendations: Initiate dopamine‑agonist therapy, preferably cabergoline 0.25 mg twice weekly with titration based on prolactin response and tolerance; bromocriptine is an alternative if cabergoline is contraindicated. Obtain baseline cardiac echocardiogram and repeat annually if cabergoline dose exceeds 2 mg/week or cumulative exposure is high. Perform macroprolactin assay to exclude assay interference before treatment. Order a full pituitary hormone panel to assess other axes and repeat at 3‑month intervals until stable. Schedule visual‑field perimetry now and repeat if symptoms evolve; repeat pituitary MRI in 6–12 months to document tumor shrinkage. Check serum prolactin in 4–6 weeks after therapy initiation, then every 3 months until normalized. Conduct baseline DEXA scan given amenorrhea, weight gain, and family history of osteoporosis; repeat every 2–3 years or sooner if indicated. Screen for depression; consider referral to mental‑health services and initiate low‑dose SSRI if depressive symptoms persist after hormonal control. Counsel the patient on lifestyle measures: regular moderate exercise, balanced nutrition, weight management, and avoidance of substances that may raise prolactin (e.g., certain herbal supplements). Educate on warning signs of pituitary apoplexy—sudden severe headache, visual loss, ophthalmoplegia—and advise immediate medical attention if they occur. Optimize headache management with acetaminophen as needed, limit NSAID use to the lowest effective dose, and consider non‑pharmacologic strategies (stress reduction, sleep hygiene). Provide pre‑conception counseling; once prolactin normalizes and menses resume, discuss timing of conception and the safety of continuing cabergoline during early pregnancy, with close obstetric‑endocrine follow‑up.  

Notes: The patient’s mild depressive symptoms may be secondary to hyperprolactinemia and chronic infertility; addressing hormonal control often improves mood. Ongoing communication between primary care, endocrinology, and reproductive specialists is essential for coordinated care.

Age: 44 years  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Progressive nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, lethargy, and refractory hypotension following viral gastroenteritis, with inability to retain oral hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone.  

Analysis: The panel reached unanimous consensus that the patient is experiencing an acute primary adrenal (Addisonian) crisis precipitated by gastrointestinal illness leading to failure of oral glucocorticoid absorption. Key red‑flag findings—refractory hypotension despite 2 L isotonic saline, severe hyponatremia (118 mEq/L), hyperkalemia (6.4 mEq/L), hypoglycemia (52 mg/dL), elevated BUN/creatinine, ECG changes, and a random cortisol of 1.2 mcg/dL—confirm glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid deficiency. The hyperpigmentation supports chronic primary adrenal insufficiency. The panel agreed on the need for ICU‑level care, Emergency Medicine leadership, and immediate endocrinology consultation. Consensus differed only on the preferred maintenance hydrocortisone regimen after the initial 100 mg bolus; one expert advocated intermittent dosing of 50 mg IV every 6–8 hours, while another supported a continuous infusion of 200 mg over 24 hours. Both approaches were deemed acceptable. Additional considerations raised during the rounds included criteria for vasopressor initiation, routine lactate and arterial blood gas monitoring, serum ACTH testing after stabilization, systematic infection work‑up, imaging for adrenal hemorrhage when indicated, thresholds for renal replacement therapy, potential use of glucagon, and the need for thorough patient and caregiver education.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Continuous cardiac monitoring, arterial line for blood pressure monitoring, point‑of‑care glucose testing, serum electrolytes, renal panel, serum cortisol, arterial blood gas with lactate, serum ACTH (post‑stabilization), blood cultures, stool studies (culture, C. difficile toxin, viral PCR panel), abdominal CT or MRI if adrenal hemorrhage is suspected, urine output measurement, and bedside ultrasound if volume status assessment is needed.  

Conclusion: Acute primary adrenal crisis precipitated by vomiting from viral gastroenteritis, resulting in life‑threatening shock and multi‑system derangements.  

Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology  

Recommendations: Initiate immediate ICU admission with airway, breathing, and circulation management led by Emergency Medicine. Administer IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus followed by either 50 mg IV every 6–8 hours or a continuous infusion of 200 mg/24 hours, with subsequent taper based on clinical response. Begin aggressive isotonic saline boluses (1–2 L) repeated as needed, adding 5 % dextrose to treat hypoglycemia. Treat hyperkalemia urgently with IV calcium gluconate, insulin with dextrose, nebulized albuterol, and consider sodium bicarbonate if metabolic acidosis is present. Withhold fludrocortisone during the acute phase because high‑dose hydrocortisone provides sufficient mineralocorticoid activity. If hypotension persists after 2–3 L fluids and steroids, start norepinephrine to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg; consider glucagon only if catecholamine resistance occurs. Obtain serum lactate and arterial blood gas on arrival and repeat to guide resuscitation. Perform a structured infection work‑up including blood cultures and stool studies; treat any identified bacterial infection per guidelines. After hemodynamic stabilization, draw serum ACTH to confirm primary versus secondary insufficiency and consider adrenal autoantibody testing if autoimmune Addison disease is suspected. Monitor renal function and urine output closely; initiate renal replacement therapy if hyperkalemia remains refractory (>6.5 mEq/L with ECG changes) or if acute kidney injury worsens with volume overload or severe acidosis. Reserve abdominal imaging for cases with atypical features or lack of response to therapy to evaluate for adrenal hemorrhage or infarction. Upon stabilization, transition to maintenance hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone dosing, provide an emergency intramuscular hydrocortisone kit, medical‑alert identification, and comprehensive sick‑day rules education for the patient and caregivers, emphasizing the need for prompt medical attention when vomiting prevents oral medication intake.  

Notes: Both intermittent and continuous hydrocortisone dosing regimens are acceptable; choice may be guided by institutional protocols and patient-specific factors. Continuous reassessment of fluid status, electrolytes, and hemodynamics is essential throughout the acute phase.

Age: 55
Sex: Male
Complaint: Rapidly worsening pain, swelling, and redness of the right lower leg with systemic toxicity following a minor abrasion.

Analysis: All three experts unanimously diagnose necrotizing fasciitis of the right lower leg, likely polymicrobial with gas‑forming organisms (Clostridium spp. or mixed anaerobes). The high LRINEC score (10), presence of crepitus, hemorrhagic bullae, dusky discoloration, severe pain out of proportion, systemic signs of sepsis, and CT evidence of gas in the fascial planes confirm the diagnosis. Consensus agrees that this is a life‑threatening surgical emergency requiring immediate source control and ICU‑level support. Divergence exists only in the sequencing of specialty involvement: Expert A suggests simultaneous early General Surgery consultation with Emergency Medicine resuscitation; Expert B and Expert C emphasize that Emergency Medicine must first stabilize the patient (airway, breathing, circulation, sepsis bundle) before the operative team proceeds. The integrated conclusion is that rapid hemodynamic stabilization by Emergency Medicine and immediate activation of General Surgery for emergent debridement are both essential and should occur in parallel, with EM leading the initial resuscitation.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: 
- Repeat complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, serum lactate, CRP, coagulation profile, serum calcium, and arterial blood gas. 
- Blood cultures (aerobic and anaerobic) and wound/tissue cultures obtained before antibiotics. 
- CT scan of the affected limb (already performed) confirming gas tracking; no further imaging required. 
- Bedside ultrasound or Doppler if compartment syndrome is suspected. 
- Continuous hemodynamic monitoring (arterial line) in the ICU.

Conclusion: Necrotizing fasciitis of the right lower leg with septic shock and acute kidney injury; requires emergent surgical debridement and intensive supportive care.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: General Surgery

Recommendations: 
- Initiate immediate ABC assessment and secure airway if needed. 
- Begin aggressive isotonic crystalloid resuscitation; target MAP ≥65 mmHg, and start norepinephrine infusion promptly if hypotension persists. 
- Obtain blood, wound, and tissue cultures before antibiotics, but do not delay antimicrobial therapy. 
- Administer empiric broad‑spectrum IV antibiotics with renal dose adjustment: vancomycin plus piperacillin‑tazobactam (or meropenem) plus clindamycin for toxin suppression. 
- Discontinue oral cephalexin; switch to the above IV regimen. 
- Provide tetanus prophylaxis (tetanus toxoid ± immunoglobulin as indicated). 
- Start continuous insulin infusion to maintain blood glucose 140‑180 mg/dL, monitoring hourly. 
- Admit to the ICU for continuous hemodynamic, renal, and metabolic monitoring. 
- Activate General Surgery for emergent operative debridement; aim for the operating room within the first hour of diagnosis. 
- Intra‑operative assessment for compartment syndrome; perform fasciotomy if indicated. 
- Plan for repeat debridements every 24‑48 hours until all necrotic tissue is removed and margins are clear. 
- Consider hyperbaric oxygen therapy as an adjunct if available and does not delay surgery. 
- Monitor renal function closely; be prepared to initiate continuous renal replacement therapy if AKI progresses. 
- Serially check CBC, CMP, lactate, CRP, coagulation profile, and serum calcium; correct hyponatremia, hypocalcemia, and other electrolyte abnormalities promptly. 
- Watch for signs of disseminated intravascular coagulation and treat according to protocol. 
- Discuss prognosis, potential limb loss, and reconstructive options (skin grafts, flaps) with the patient and family early; involve plastic surgery and rehabilitation services as needed. 
- Document all interventions and communicate continuously among Emergency Medicine, Critical Care, General Surgery, Infectious Diseases, and ancillary services.

Notes: The rapid progression of necrotizing fasciitis mandates that no further diagnostic delay occurs after CT confirmation. All care steps should be coordinated in parallel to minimize time to source control. Continuous reassessment for hemodynamic stability, organ dysfunction, and wound status is essential throughout the hospital course.

case_text:
Vignette:
A 20-year-old male college athlete presents with itchy, peeling skin between his toes bilaterally for the past 2 weeks. He plays on the soccer team and uses communal showers at the athletic facility daily. He denies pain, swelling, or spreading beyond the interdigital spaces. He has no history of diabetes or immunosuppression. On examination, there is maceration and peeling of the skin in the third and fourth interdigital web spaces of both feet. Mild erythema is present. There are no vesicles, bullae, or fissures extending to the soles. Toenails appear normal.

winner_protocol:
Age: 20 years  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Itchy, peeling skin between the third and fourth toes on both feet for 2 weeks; no pain, swelling, or spread beyond interdigital spaces.  

Analysis: All three experts unanimously diagnosed classic interdigital tinea pedis (athlete’s foot) caused most commonly by Trichophyton rubrum or T. interdigitale. The presentation—bilateral maceration, peeling, mild erythema in a young athlete who uses communal showers—is textbook for dermatophyte infection, and no atypical features (vesicles, purulence, systemic signs) were noted. Consensus agrees the condition is non‑urgent and can be managed electively with topical antifungal therapy; red‑flag signs (severe pain, extensive swelling, purulent discharge, fever, rapid progression, immunocompromise, diabetes, cellulitis) would mandate urgent evaluation. All experts recommend topical azole or allylamine agents applied twice daily for 2–4 weeks, no routine laboratory testing, and reserve systemic therapy or dermatology referral for refractory disease, nail involvement, or diagnostic uncertainty.  

Where consensus differed: Expert C initially labeled the emergency type as “Requires non‑emergent care” (a phrasing variation) whereas the Delphi consensus label is “Self‑care appropriate.” Expert C also emphasized Dermatology as the primary managing specialty, while Expert B described referral as optional and non‑urgent. These nuances are incorporated into the recommendations.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None required for typical presentation. Reserve potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation or fungal culture if lesions are atypical, fail to improve after 2–4 weeks, or if secondary infection is suspected.  

Conclusion: Interdigital tinea pedis (athlete’s foot) – self‑care appropriate.  

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology  

Recommendations: Initiate topical antifungal therapy with clotrimazole 1 % or miconazole 2 % cream, or terbinafine 1 % cream, applied to the affected web spaces twice daily for a total of 2–4 weeks, continuing for several days after symptom resolution to prevent relapse. Counsel the patient on strict foot hygiene: keep feet dry, change socks at least daily, use moisture‑wicking or cotton socks, wear breathable athletic shoes and rotate footwear to allow drying, apply antifungal powder or spray to shoes and feet, wear shower shoes in communal areas, avoid sharing towels or footwear, and trim toenails straight across. Assess footwear habits and advise against tight, non‑breathable shoes that maintain moisture. Monitor for secondary bacterial infection—watch for increasing pain, warmth, swelling, or purulent discharge—and for early nail changes that may signal onychomycosis. Advise the patient to avoid topical steroids, which can mask the infection and produce “tinea incognito.” If lesions spread to other body sites (e.g., tinea corporis, cruris) or if there is suspicion of Candida intertrigo, evaluate accordingly. Re‑evaluate in 2–4 weeks; if the rash persists, obtain KOH preparation or culture, consider a stronger topical formulation, or initiate systemic antifungal therapy (e.g., oral terbinafine) and arrange dermatology referral for persistent, recurrent, or nail‑involved disease.  

Notes: Expect symptomatic improvement within 3–7 days; full clinical resolution typically occurs within 2–4 weeks with adherence. Document any red‑flag signs promptly and adjust management.
